questions.prompt: What do the extrinsic muscles of the eye control?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Movement of the eyeball
questions.suggestedRationale: Extrinsic eye muscles move the eyeball in the orbit.

questions.prompt: The following happens for the pupil of the eye to dilate
options: he circular muscle of the iris must contract.
Cranial nerve III must be activated.
Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system is required
The optic nerve must be stimulated.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system is required
questions.suggestedRationale: Pupillary dilation is a sympathetic effect; CN III constricts the pupil.

questions.prompt: Trachoma is caused by _________ is a ________ infection
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Chlamydia bacteria and eye
questions.suggestedRationale: Trachoma is a Chlamydia trachomatis infection of the eye.

questions.prompt: Which statement does NOT apply to chronic glaucoma?
options: Degeneration and obstruction of the trabecular network
Abnormally narrow angle between the cornea and iris
Damage to the retina and optic nerve
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Abnormally narrow angle between the cornea and iris
questions.suggestedRationale: A narrow cornea–iris angle describes acute (closed-angle) glaucoma, not chronic open-angle glaucoma.

questions.prompt: Chronic Glaucoma results in
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Loss of peripheral vision
questions.suggestedRationale: Chronic glaucoma typically produces gradual loss of peripheral vision.

questions.prompt: True or False: Cataract is the gradual clouding of the lens of the eye
questions.suggestedLabel: A. True
questions.suggestedRationale: A cataract is gradual clouding of the lens—true.

questions.prompt: Inner Ear contains the?
options: Organ of Corti and Semicircular Canals
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Organ of Corti and Semicircular Canals
questions.suggestedRationale: The inner ear contains the cochlea (organ of Corti) and the semicircular canals; ossicles are middle ear.

questions.prompt: What is Conduction Deafness
options: Damage to the organ of Corti
Adhesions reducing the movement of the ossicles.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Adhesions reducing the movement of the ossicles.
questions.suggestedRationale: Conduction deafness can result from ossicles that no longer move freely (otosclerosis or adhesions).

questions.prompt: Certain drugs or chemicals can be ototoxic and the first sign of ototoxicity is?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Tinnitus
questions.suggestedRationale: Tinnitus is usually the first warning of ototoxicity.

questions.prompt: What would a patient with early stages of age related macular degeneration present with?
options: Loss of night vision and color perception
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Loss of central visual acuity
questions.suggestedRationale: Early age-related macular degeneration reduces central visual acuity.

questions.prompt: An infection that damages the auditory nerve can cause what type of hearing loss?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Sensorineural
questions.suggestedRationale: Damage to the auditory nerve causes sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.prompt: Which fluid is found surrounding the optic disc?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Cerebrospinal fluid
questions.suggestedRationale: CSF surrounds the optic disc, which is why high ICP causes papilledema.

questions.prompt: What role does Fovea Centralis Play?
options: Maintain Occular Pressure and balance ICP
Protects the Iris and the Lens
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Provides the greatest Visual Acuity
questions.suggestedRationale: The fovea centralis is the site of sharpest visual acuity.

questions.prompt: The lens and cornea are nourished by
questions.suggestedLabel: D. aqueous humor.
questions.suggestedRationale: The avascular lens and cornea are nourished by aqueous humor.

questions.prompt: A patient presents with Trachoma, the nurse understands that Trachoma in patients is presented by?
options: corneal abrasions by the infected eyelids.
ptosis and fixed dilation of the pupil.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. corneal abrasions by the infected eyelids.
questions.suggestedRationale: Trachoma scars and inverts the lids so lashes abrade the cornea.

questions.prompt: Which of the statements apply to infection of the eye by Staphylococcus aureus?
options: It usually causes keratitis and permanent visual loss.
questions.suggestedRationale: Staph conjunctivitis (pinkeye) involves the conjunctiva and is highly contagious; it does not usually cause permanent visual loss.

questions.prompt: A patient presents to the ER with Corneal Ulceration and Scarring- The nurse assesses the patient and realizes that a potential cause for this could be?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Herpes Simplex Virus
questions.suggestedRationale: Herpes simplex keratitis is a classic cause of corneal ulceration and scarring.

questions.prompt: Sensory receptors that provide information about body movement, orientation, or muscle stretch are referred to as
questions.suggestedLabel: D. proprioceptors.
questions.suggestedRationale: Proprioceptors sense joint position, movement, and muscle stretch.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical transmitter released at the neuromuscular junction?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Acetylcholine
questions.suggestedRationale: Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.prompt: What are the two types of bone tissue?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Compact and cancellous
questions.suggestedRationale: The two bone tissues are compact and cancellous (spongy).

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a Colles’ fracture?
options: A spontaneous fracture occurs in weakened bone.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. The distal radius is broken.
questions.suggestedRationale: A Colles fracture is a break of the distal radius.

questions.prompt: The presence of a hematoma during the healing process:
options: is broken down and absorbed immediately.
provides the base for bone cells to produce new bone.
is the structure into which granulation tissue grows.
produces fibroblasts to lay down new cartilage.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. is the structure into which granulation tissue grows.
questions.suggestedRationale: The fracture hematoma is the framework into which granulation tissue grows.

questions.prompt: When a fracture is healing, the procallus or fibrocartilaginous callus- select all that applies
options: serves as a splint across the fracture site
is the tissue that lays down new cartilage.
is made up of new bone.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. serves as a splint across the fracture site
questions.suggestedRationale: The fibrocartilaginous (procallus) callus acts as a splint and cannot bear weight; the form listed no combined option.

questions.prompt: The inflammation surrounding a fracture site during the first few days may complicate healing by causing
questions.suggestedLabel: B. severe ischemia and tissue necrosis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Marked inflammation around a fracture can compromise blood flow and cause ischemia or necrosis.

questions.prompt: Select All that apply- All of the following predispose to osteoporosis
questions.suggestedLabel: B. a sedentary lifestyle.
questions.suggestedRationale: A sedentary lifestyle, long-term glucocorticoids, and calcium deficit predispose to osteoporosis; weight-bearing activity is protective. No combined choice was listed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements does NOT apply to osteoporosis?
options: Bone resorption is greater than bone formation.
It causes compression fractures of the vertebrae.
Osteoporosis is always a primary disorder.
It often leads to kyphosis and loss of height.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Osteoporosis is always a primary disorder.
questions.suggestedRationale: Osteoporosis can be secondary, so it is not always a primary disorder.

questions.prompt: Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy is or are ? (select all that apply)
options: Is a X-Linked recessive genetic disease
There is difficulty climbing stairs or standing up at 2 to 3 years of age.
It involves only the legs and pelvis.
Skeletal muscle atrophy can be seen in the legs of a toddler.
It cannot be detected in any carriers.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Is a X-Linked recessive genetic disease
questions.suggestedRationale: Duchenne dystrophy is X-linked recessive and shows Gower/stair difficulty at ages 2–3; it is not limited to the legs, and calves are pseudohypertrophic. The form had no combined key.

questions.prompt: Osteo Sarcoma presents with:
options: Steady, severe, and persisting with rest
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Steady, severe, and persisting with rest
questions.suggestedRationale: Osteosarcoma pain is typically steady, deep, and persists at rest.

questions.prompt: Osteoarthritis pain presents with
options: Quite severe in the early stages
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Increased with weight-bearing and activity
questions.suggestedRationale: Osteoarthritis pain is worse with weight-bearing and activity.

questions.prompt: What limits mobility in Osteoarthritis ?
options: Inflammation and fibrosis develop at the joints.
Degeneration of articulating cartilage occurs in the large joints.
It progresses bilaterally through the small joints.
There are no changes in the bone at the affected joints.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Degeneration of articulating cartilage occurs in the large joints.
questions.suggestedRationale: OA limits motion because articular cartilage in large weight-bearing joints degenerates.

questions.prompt: A key to identifying Rheumatoid Arthritis is in how it presents itself is or are: ( could be more than 1 choice)
options: Random single joints, progressing to involve other joints
Bilateral small joints, symmetrical progression to other joints
Abused or damaged joints first, then joints damaged by compensatory movement
Systemic inflammatory disorder due to an autoimmune reaction
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Bilateral small joints, symmetrical progression to other joints
questions.suggestedRationale: RA typically starts in bilateral, symmetric small joints and is a systemic autoimmune disease; the form offered no combined choice.

questions.prompt: Ankylosis and deformity develop in rheumatoid arthritis because
questions.suggestedLabel: B. fibrosis occurs in the joint.
questions.suggestedRationale: Fibrosis in the joint produces ankylosis and deformity (tendon shortening also contributes).

questions.prompt: Signs and Symptoms of systemic effect of Rheumatoid Arthritis are?
options: nodules in various tissues, severe fatigue, and anorexia.
swelling and dysfunction in many organs.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. nodules in various tissues, severe fatigue, and anorexia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Systemic RA features include rheumatoid nodules, fatigue, and anorexia.

questions.prompt: A precipitating factor for Gout is
options: A sudden increase in serum uric acid levels
questions.suggestedLabel: A. A sudden increase in serum uric acid levels
questions.suggestedRationale: A sudden rise in serum uric acid can precipitate an acute gout attack.

questions.prompt: Individuals living with ankylosing spondylitis- the diseases begins with
options: Costovertebral joints with progression down the spine
Cervical and thoracic vertebrae, causing kyphosis
Sacroiliac joints with progression up the spine
Peripheral joints and then proceeds to the vertebrae
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Sacroiliac joints with progression up the spine
questions.suggestedRationale: Ankylosing spondylitis usually starts in the sacroiliac joints and ascends the spine.

questions.prompt: Major complication from a Fat Emboli from a broken long bone is
options: Additional ischemia in the broken bone
Nonunion or malunion of the fracture
Pulmonary inflammation and obstruction or embolus
Abscess and infection at a distant site
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Pulmonary inflammation and obstruction or embolus
questions.suggestedRationale: Fat emboli from long-bone fractures lodge in the lungs and cause inflammation and vascular obstruction.

questions.prompt: The distinguishing feature of primary fibromyalgia syndrome is
options: Joint pain and stiffness throughout the body
Degeneration and atrophy of skeletal muscles in back and lower limbs
Specific trigger points for pain and tenderness
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Specific trigger points for pain and tenderness
questions.suggestedRationale: Fibromyalgia is characterized by specific tender/trigger points.

questions.prompt: Ewing’s sarcoma metastasizes at an early stage to the
questions.suggestedLabel: C. lungs.
questions.suggestedRationale: Ewing sarcoma tends to metastasize early to the lungs.

questions.prompt: Rickets disease is:
options: a deficit of vitamin D and phosphates.
replacement of bone by fibrous tissue.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. a deficit of vitamin D and phosphates.
questions.suggestedRationale: Rickets is caused by a deficit of vitamin D and phosphate, impairing mineralization.

questions.prompt: Paget’s disease often leads to which of the following?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Cardiovascular disease
questions.suggestedRationale: Paget disease of bone can lead to high-output cardiovascular disease.

questions.prompt: The type of compound fracture in which there are multiple fracture lines and bone fragments is referred to as a/an
questions.suggestedLabel: D. comminuted fracture
questions.suggestedRationale: A comminuted fracture has multiple fracture lines and fragments.

questions.prompt: Fluid-filled sacs composed of synovial membrane located between structures such as tendons and ligaments and act as additional cushions are called
questions.suggestedLabel: B. bursae.
questions.suggestedRationale: Bursae are synovial-lined sacs that cushion tendons and ligaments.

questions.prompt: In which structure do pain impulses ascend the spinal cord?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Spinothalamic tract
questions.suggestedRationale: Pain impulses ascend the cord in the spinothalamic tract.

questions.prompt: According to the gate-control theory, passage of pain impulses may be naturally blocked
options: at the synapse by entry of other sensory impulses.
by administration of morphine directly into the spinal cord.
by referring the pain to other parts of the body.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. at the synapse by entry of other sensory impulses.
questions.suggestedRationale: Gate control: competing sensory input can block pain transmission at the spinal synapse.

questions.prompt: What is the definition of endorphins?
options: Opiate-like blocking agents in the central nervous system
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Opiate-like blocking agents in the central nervous system
questions.suggestedRationale: Endorphins are endogenous, opiate-like pain-blocking peptides in the CNS.

questions.prompt: Which of the following applies to spinal anesthesia?
options: It causes analgesia with loss of consciousness.
The drug is injected into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or the epidural space of the spinal cord.
The drug stimulates release of endorphins in the spinal cord.
The transmission of pain impulses is blocked in a small area of the body.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. The drug is injected into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or the epidural space of the spinal cord.
questions.suggestedRationale: Spinal or epidural anesthesia is injected into the CSF or epidural space and does not cause unconsciousness.

questions.prompt: What is the role of nociceptors?
options: pain receptors that are stimulated by thermal, chemical, or physical means.
spinal nerves that conduct impulses from specific areas of the skin.
responsible for the state of arousal with pain.
useful in localizing pain to a specific area of the body.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. pain receptors that are stimulated by thermal, chemical, or physical means.
questions.suggestedRationale: Nociceptors are pain receptors activated by thermal, chemical, or mechanical stimuli.

questions.prompt: Pain that is caused by trauma or disease involving the peripheral nerves is referred to as
questions.suggestedLabel: A. neuropathic pain.
questions.suggestedRationale: Pain from disease or trauma of peripheral nerves is neuropathic pain.

questions.prompt: Opioids released within the central nervous system are secreted by
questions.suggestedLabel: D. interneurons.
questions.suggestedRationale: CNS opioid peptides (enkephalins/endorphins) are released by interneurons.

questions.prompt: The release of neuropeptides due to a reduction in serotonin is often the cause of
questions.suggestedLabel: A. migraine.
questions.suggestedRationale: Migraine is linked to falling serotonin and release of vasoactive neuropeptides.
